name: Erik Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for fitting me in, Erik. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say is confidential and won't carry your name. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: There are two kinds of day. On a normal one, I'm with a trouble crew for the power company along the coast, driving round fixing faults, a blown fuse here, a line some delivery truck pulled down there. Then there are storm days, when the wind comes off the sea and we work sixteen hours straight putting the coast back together.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like storm work, weirdly, even though it's brutal. People come out of their houses with coffee when you get their lights back on, and the overtime is great. What wears me out is being the new guy, I did three years roofing before this, so I'm good with heights but still clumsy with the electrical side. My foreman, Dee, double-checks everything I do, which is fair, but it gets in your head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fair enough, it was oversold. I'd probably say it to my housemate Jonas, who's been telling me for two years that AI will take over everything. Online I don't really post, I just read.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my life carries on as planned. I finish my apprenticeship, I keep picking up storm overtime, and maybe I buy a better motorbike. Honestly the biggest change AI made for me is it writes the polite emails to my landlord.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going. Keep doing the overtime when the storms come, keep around two and a half months of money in the bank, which goes up and down with the weather. Keep using the AI thing for emails and the odd question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe a bit pleased I can tell Jonas he was wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your savings go up and down with the weather. How does that work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In a bad storm season I can make an extra few thousand in overtime. Last winter I put most of it in savings, the winter before I put most of it into the motorbike. So it depends on the season and on how sensible I'm being.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything here that would bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe that the company still uses AI to predict where storms will hit, which could mean fewer guys on standby. But if it's only small stuff like that, I'm not losing sleep.

S0.say: I'd say fair enough, it was oversold. I'd mostly say it to my housemate Jonas, who's been telling me AI will take over everything.
S0.think: It means my life carries on as planned: finish the apprenticeship, keep doing storm overtime, maybe buy a better motorbike. AI's biggest change for me is writing polite emails to my landlord.
S0.do: Keeps working as normal and takes storm overtime when it comes. Holds around two and a half months of savings and keeps using AI now and then for emails.
S0.feel: Calm, and a little pleased to prove his housemate wrong.
S0.quote: Honestly the biggest change AI made for me is it writes the polite emails to my landlord.
S0.fieldNote: Erik's money swings with the storm season, and he's honest that his savings depend on how sensible he's been. He uses AI casually for small things and doesn't think about it much. The only thing he flags is the company using forecasting to trim standby crews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change and people should take it seriously, but not panic. At work I'd say we'll still be needed when the poles come down in a storm. I'd want the company and the government both to do their part, not just leave it to us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I don't think the climbing goes away, but I think the overtime does. If AI gets really good at predicting storms and routing crews, the company won't keep twelve guys on standby, they'll keep eight. The storm money is what lets me save, so losing it is like a pay cut nobody announces.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop counting on overtime and save more from my base pay, maybe an extra hundred a week. I'd look at what the guys who get picked for the new kit are doing differently and learn it once it's clear it works. I'd wait a year before making any big move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's not a disaster, it's just a slow leak.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the motorbike money in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the old bike and put the money aside. It's fine, it runs. The new one was always more of a want than a need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dee, maybe, my foreman. She's great at reading a storm and knowing where to send people, and that's exactly what the AI would be doing. I don't know what a foreman does if the computer plans the day.

S1.say: I'd say it's a big change to take seriously without panicking, and we'll still be needed when poles come down. I'd want the company and government both to do their part.
S1.think: I don't think the climbing goes away, but the overtime might, if AI plans storm crews more tightly. Storm money is what lets me save, so losing it is a pay cut nobody announces.
S1.do: Stops counting on overtime and saves about an extra hundred a week from base pay. Keeps his old motorbike, watches who gets picked for new equipment and learns those tools once they're proven.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like a slow leak rather than a disaster.
S1.quote: The storm money is what lets me save, so losing it is like a pay cut nobody announces.
S1.fieldNote: His threat is specific and financial: the storm overtime that funds his savings. He'd watch colleagues before adopting anything, which fits his wait-until-proven style. He worries most for his foreman, whose skill at reading storms is the kind of planning AI could take over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is going way too fast and somebody needs to slow it down, I don't care who. At work I'd say keep your heads down and do good work. I'd probably talk about it more with Jonas and my brother than with anyone at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be worried. A private company will grab the cheapest option the second it's available, and I'm the cheapest guy to let go because I'm still learning. I think storm work at night will be the last thing robots do well, but two years doesn't leave much room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sell the motorbike, that's an easy few thousand, and get the savings to four or five months. I'd apply to the public utility in the next town, because I think a public company would move slower and keep people longer. I'd keep doing every storm shift I could while they still needed us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicked, but definitely pacing the kitchen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you think the public utility would keep people longer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just from what I've seen, they move slower on everything. They took five years to switch to the new meters, our company did it in one. In this picture, slow and boring is exactly what I'd want my boss to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your brother?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My brother's a chef. I'd probably say at least people still want to eat a meal a person cooked, and he'd say, have you seen the robot burger places? We'd laugh, but it wouldn't be very funny.

S2.say: I'd say this is moving way too fast and somebody needs to slow it down, whoever that is. At work I'd tell people to keep their heads down and do good work.
S2.think: I'd be worried, because a private company grabs the cheapest option, and I'm the cheapest guy to let go. Storm work at night may be the last thing robots do well, but two years doesn't leave much room.
S2.do: Sells his motorbike to push savings to four or five months. Applies to the public utility in the next town, expecting it to keep people longer, and takes every storm shift he can.
S2.feel: Anxious, pacing the kitchen but not panicking.
S2.quote: In this picture, slow and boring is exactly what I'd want my boss to be.
S2.fieldNote: Erik's practical move is to switch from a private to a public employer, betting on slowness. He's clear-eyed that being junior makes him easy to cut. He has a sense of humour about it with his brother, but admits it wouldn't feel funny.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to plan if people start now. At work I'd say let's find out what the company wants us to learn and get on with it. I'd stay away from the shouting online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is about right for me to get my full qualification and a couple of years' experience. Then I think the useful people will be the ones who understand substations and protection systems, the brains of the grid. I'd want to be one of them, but only once I see that's where the jobs actually go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year, I'd finish my apprenticeship hours and keep my savings around four months. By year two, if the company's hiring for substation and protection roles, I'd apply for that training. I'd sell the bike only if things got tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'd have a plan, which helps a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a protection systems person do, in simple words?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They set up the equipment that cuts power when something goes wrong, so a fault doesn't burn down a street. It's part electrician, part computer. I used to think it was the boring job. In this picture it's the job I'd want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep the bike unless things got tight. Isn't that a contradiction with saving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha, yeah, maybe. It's my one fun thing. I'd keep it as long as the savings are above three months, that's my line.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to plan if people start now, so let's find out what the company wants us to learn. I'd stay away from the shouting online.
S3.think: Five years lets me qualify and get experience, and then I think the substation and protection people, the brains of the grid, will be needed. I'd want to be one of them once I see that's where jobs go.
S3.do: Finishes his apprenticeship hours and holds about four months of savings. Applies for substation and protection training in year two if the company is hiring for it, keeping his motorbike unless savings drop below three months.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but having a plan helps a lot.
S3.quote: I used to think it was the boring job. In this picture it's the job I'd want.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns his worry into a plan with a clear trigger: hiring for protection roles. He admits the motorbike contradiction cheerfully and sets himself a rule about it. His centre outlook shows in avoiding the online shouting and simply asking what the company needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, so let's use it sensibly. At work I'd say this is the time to get qualified in more than one thing. To friends I'd say it's real, but it's not tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels fine for me. I'd be thirty-seven, I'd have my ticket, protection training and years on storm crews. Whatever happens after that, I'd have had a good run and I'd have time to see what the next thing is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the normal path, finish the apprenticeship and do storm overtime, and save most of it this time, not spend it. In year three or four I'd do the protection training. I'd stay with my company unless it started to look shaky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Ten years is a whole other life away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said ten years is a whole other life. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years ago I was seventeen and wanted to be a racing driver. Ten years from now I could be anything, so I'm not going to lose sleep over a robot that hasn't been built yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of this picture that still bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe what happens to the older guys who have no time to switch. Dee's in her fifties, she'd be retiring around then, so she's probably okay, but some of the guys in their forties would be stuck. I'd be fine. It's the forty-five-year-old with two kids I'd worry about.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a long time, so let's use it sensibly and get qualified in more than one thing. It's real, but it's not tomorrow.
S4.think: Ten years feels fine for me: I'd be thirty-seven with my ticket, protection training and storm experience. Whatever comes after, I'd have time to see the next thing.
S4.do: Finishes his apprenticeship, takes storm overtime and saves most of it. Does protection training in year three or four and stays with his company unless it looks shaky.
S4.feel: Mostly calm, as ten years feels like a whole other life away.
S4.quote: I'd be fine. It's the forty-five-year-old with two kids I'd worry about.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Erik relaxes completely about himself, pointing out that ten years ago he wanted to be a racing driver. His concern shifts to colleagues in their forties with children. He'd still follow the same practical training path, just more slowly.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because a private company would move faster than I can learn. What would help is the company being straight with us early about which jobs are going, and paying for training into the jobs that stay. I don't need a lot, just a heads-up.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about storms getting worse. Every year the storms here are bigger. Whatever AI does, the weather's still going to knock lines down, and for a while somebody still has to go out in it.

headlineQuote: Ten years from now I could be anything, so I'm not going to lose sleep over a robot that hasn't been built yet.
portrait: Erik is a 27-year-old apprentice on a coastal trouble crew who spent three years roofing before switching to lines, good with heights but still clumsy on the electrical side. He uses AI now and then for emails and lives on storm overtime, which swings his savings up and down. He's calm about the plateau, uneasy that steady disruption would quietly cut his overtime, and anxious about the two-year AGI picture, where he'd try to move to a slower public utility. With five or ten years he plans a move into substation and protection work and becomes calm about himself, worrying instead for older colleagues with children.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because a private company would move faster than he could learn.
whatWouldHelp: The company being honest early about which jobs are going and paying for training into the jobs that stay.
